text: Traditional dentures, snap-in dentures on implants, or fixed teeth that never come out: the ways to replace a full arch, compared by a prosthodontist, the dental specialist in replacing teeth.
A denture that fit last year can rub this year.

Without tooth roots to load it, the jawbone under a denture keeps receding, so the fit loosens. A loose denture rubs, needs adhesive, limits what you eat and has to be relined, and over years the bone loss changes the shape of the face.
Four ways to deal with dentures.
Acrylic teeth on a base that rests on the gums. The lowest cost, but they move, need relines and repairs, must come out to clean, and do nothing to stop bone loss.
A removable denture that clips onto two or more implants. It stops slipping, puts load back into the bone and still comes out for cleaning: around 60% of natural function at a moderate cost.
Teeth that never come out: a zirconia bridge screwed onto four to eight implants, often All-on-4 with provisional teeth the same day. Over 98% of natural function, at the highest cost.
A broken or damaged denture is one of the emergencies the practice makes room for, the same day wherever possible.

faq: Because the jawbone they rest on keeps receding once the teeth are gone, and nothing loads it. A reline refits the denture for a while; anchoring it to implants stops the movement.
Implant-supported dentures: a removable denture that clips onto two or more implants, so it stops slipping but still comes out for cleaning.
Can I go from dentures to fixed teeth?

Yes. Bone loss from years of wearing a denture often makes you a candidate for All-on-4 rather than ruling you out, and in most cases you leave the surgery wearing fixed provisional teeth. Some mouths need bone grafting first.
